1. Pyoderma gangrenosum (ulcerative neutrophilic dermatosis) — favored by painful necrolytic ulcers with mucosal extension, neutrophil-rich infiltrate with leukocytoclasis and “cryptococcoid” (degenerated neutrophil) forms and negative cultures.
2. Cutaneous leukocytoclastic (small-vessel) vasculitis — supported by perivascular neutrophils, karyorrhexis, extravasated erythrocytes and fibrinoid vessel necrosis (possible drug- or immune-complex–mediated).
3. ANCA-associated vasculitis (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangiitis) with cutaneous involvement — can produce mucocutaneous ulceration and small/medium-vessel necrotizing vasculitis; consider given mucosal involvement.
4. Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) with secondary leukocytoclastic change — neutrophil-predominant histology and leukocytosis fit; clinical pattern may overlap with PG.
5. Invasive cutaneous fungal infection (Cryptococcus, Mucorales or other deep mycoses) — considered because of cryptococcoid-appearing forms and necrosis, but less likely given negative fungal stains and cultures.

Recommended next steps (to confirm/rule out): ANCA (c-ANCA/PR3 and p-ANCA/MPO), complement levels and urinalysis (renal involvement), review medication list for possible culprits (hydralazine), targeted blood cultures/serial cultures if systemic infection suspected, and dermatology/immunology consultation for management (avoid surgical debridement in probable PG; consider systemic immunosuppression).
ground_truth: Drug-induced ANCA vasculitis secondary to hydralazine
